Title: Describing nonstationary data streams in the frequency domain - ScienceDirect
*Concept drift* remains one of the primary challenges for the data stream processing methods. A critical challenge in processing data streams is the nonstationarity of the processed distributions — the *concept drifts* [2], which may lead to the loss of the method’s recognition abilities. While the *concept drift* has become one of the primary difficulties faced by data stream processing methods, some other limitations related to the velocity and volume of the data remain equally important. Therefore, providing the *explanation* of concept drifts in already collected data streams – including their moments, severity, and dynamics [13] – could benefit the quality of the methods’ evaluation. This work proposes the *Frequency Filtering Metadescriptor* (ffm) – a method for unsupervised data stream characterization that extracts the most informative frequency components visible in the feature vector of each processed sample, approximated at the level of a data chunk. A post-hoc application of ffm could allow for concept drift explanation [13] or annotation of real-world data streams [14]. This work describes the *Frequency Filtering Metadescriptor* – a method that extracts a *metadescription* of a data stream using informative frequency components to describe changes in the processed concepts. The *concept identification* in the real-world data streams, followed by an experiment presenting classification quality when processing the data with concept-adapted classifiers. The rest of the work is organized as follows: Section 2 describes the related works, focusing on the strategies of data stream metadescription used in the literature; Section 3 describes the method and expands on the intuition behind frequency analysis; Section 4 describes the design of experiments and their goals; Section 5 analyzes the obtained results; Section 6 presents the analysis of real-world insects data streams [10] using the proposed approach. This work proposes a tool for analyzing high-dimensional data streams in the frequency domain, allowing for *post-hoc* concept identification and visualization of the data stream. ### Concept drift detection in data stream mining: a literature review. ### Detecting group concept drift from multiple data streams. ### SDDM: an interpretable statistical concept drift detection method for data streams. ### Recurrent concept drifts on data streams.

results.title: Describing Nonstationary Data Streams in Frequency Domain
results.content:
Title: Describing Nonstationary Data Streams in Frequency Domain
The presented solution is capable of generating a *metadescription* of the data stream, separating chunks into groups describing specific concepts on its basis, and visualizing the frequencies in the original spatial domain. This work proposes the Frequency Filtering Metadescriptor – a method for unsupervised data stream characterization that extracts the most informative frequency components visible in the feature vector of each processed sample, approximated on the level of a data chunk. The rest of the work is organized as follows: Section 2 describes the related works, focusing on the strategies of data stream metadescription used in the literature; Section 3 describes the method and expands on the intuition behind frequency analysis; Section 4 describes the design of experiments and their goals; Section 5 analyses the obtained results; Section 6 presents the analysis of real-world insects data streams [10] with the proposed approach. In the first experiment, the data streams were characterized by various chunk sizes – from 50 to 200 samples in each chunk – and various numbers of drifts – from a single drift to nine sudden concept changes throughout the entire course of the stream. Similarly to the approach adopted in the first experiment, the obtained representation was normalized and clustered with *k-means* to an actual number of concepts present in the data stream, equivalent to 4444 (number of drifts +11+1+ 1). The final experiment focused on the proposed ffm approach, evaluating its ability to describe the high-dimensional data streams by identifying the number of concepts present in the given period. For this purpose, the insects data streams [10] were analyzed in a framework following the processing scheme of (a) extracting the metadescription of a data stream with ffm (b) identifying of the number of concepts present in the stream based on k-means clustering and silhouette score maximization, and (c) separating the stream into specific concepts. The presented experiments showed that the proposed approach allows for concept identification competitive with the baseline of pca feature extraction and statistically significantly better than state-of-the-art adapted in the concept drift detection and data stream classification tasks. In the final experiment, the ffm method showed the ability to identify the number of concepts present in the data stream.

results.title: [Literature Review] Describing Nonstationary Data Streams in Frequency Domain
results.content:
Title: [Literature Review] Describing Nonstationary Data Streams in Frequency Domain
## [Literature Review] Describing Nonstationary Data Streams in Frequency Domain. # [Literature Review] Describing Nonstationary Data Streams in Frequency Domain. AITackle concept drift in nonstationary streams using a novel frequency-domain method to reveal critical patterns and characterizations. The paper titled "Describing Nonstationary Data Streams in Frequency Domain" by Joanna Komorniczak addresses the issue of concept drift in data streams, which refers to the shifts in the underlying data distribution over time, affecting the performance of classifiers that rely on outdated information. The core contribution of this work is the introduction of the Frequency Filtering Metadescriptor (ffm), a tool designed for the unsupervised characterization of data streams by focusing on the frequency components that exhibit significant variance across the data. The proposed methodology employs techniques from signal processing, particularly the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT), to analyze the data streams in the frequency domain. This results in a frequency representation of the data chunk. Informative frequencies are those which contribute significantly to understanding the data stream's characteristics. **Frequency Selection**: The n frequency components with the highest variances are selected, forming a minimal yet effective representation of the data for further analysis. **Concept Clustering (Optional)**: If clustering is required, the k-means algorithm is applied to the selected frequencies to segment the chunks into distinct concepts. This allows the visualization of how specific frequencies influence the data samples. **Evaluating the influence of the number of frequency components (n)** on concept identification. The silhouette score was used to determine the optimal number of clusters, allowing for analysis of how effectively the ffm could detect recurring concepts in a data stream. The results indicated that ffm allows for competitive concept identification compared to PCA (Principal Component Analysis) and confirms its capability to effectively analyze high-dimensional data streams, particularly where traditional methods may struggle due to the curse of dimensionality. The technique was applied to real-world data streams derived from entomological studies, demonstrating the practical applicability of ffm in extracting meaningful patterns and handling variations in concept representation in nonstationary environments. In summary, the Frequency Filtering Metadescriptor (ffm) showcases a robust approach to analyzing nonstationary data streams in the frequency domain, benefiting from the inherent generalization capabilities of frequency analysis.
